Name: relation_key_indexing
Title: Facts Have Keys: Are LLM Knowledge Retrieval Keys Direction-Blind, and Can We Make Them Reversible?
Short Hypothesis: LLMs store relational facts (A, r, B) using an internal 'retrieval key' that is derived almost entirely from the source entity A plus the relation r, and is NOT indexed by the target entity B. This asymmetric key structure mechanistically explains the reversal curse (knowing 'A's mother is B' but not 'B's child is A') and predicts a broad family of retrieval failures: any query whose surface cue does not reconstruct the stored key fails, even when the fact is present. We hypothesize (1) the key is a linearly identifiable direction computed at the source-entity/relation positions, (2) reverse and paraphrased queries fail precisely when they cannot regenerate this key, and (3) a lightweight 'key-alignment' intervention that maps a reverse query onto the stored forward key restores retrieval without weight edits or retraining.
Related Work: The reversal curse (Berglund et al. 2023) documents behaviorally that models trained on 'A is B' fail on 'B is A', and follow-ups attribute it to training-order/gradient asymmetries; recent structural-hallucination work (ReGA, Noel & Seidou 2026) detects directional/role-reversal errors post hoc via graph matching but is not mechanistic. Factual-recall circuit work (Geva et al. 2023; Fierro et al. 2024) dissects subject-attribute recall as MLP-enrichment plus attention-extraction using only forward declarative queries and does not characterize an addressing 'key' or its directional asymmetry. Knowledge-editing (ROME/MEMIT) writes new associations but does not model the read-side key that determines which queries can access a stored fact. Our contribution is to reframe retrieval as key-based addressing: we (a) extract and validate a concrete internal retrieval-key direction, (b) show its source-plus-relation, target-blind structure causally produces the reversal curse and paraphrase failures, and (c) provide a read-side key-alignment intervention distinct from any training-order fix or weight edit.
Abstract: Language models retrieve stored facts by matching a query against something like an internal address. We propose that this address—the retrieval key for a relational fact (A, r, B)—is computed from the source entity A and relation r and is largely blind to the target B. This single asymmetry, we argue, mechanistically explains the reversal curse and a wider class of query-dependent retrieval failures: a query succeeds only if it reconstructs the stored forward key. We test three claims. First, using activation patching and linear probing on relational facts the model answers correctly in the forward direction, we identify a low-dimensional key direction at the source/relation positions and show that patching this key alone (not the target) is sufficient to transport the answer, while target-derived signals are not. Second, we show reverse queries ('who is B the mother of?') and indirect paraphrases fail exactly when they produce a key that is far (in cosine similarity) from the stored forward key; key-distance predicts per-example reverse-recall failure with high AUROC, beyond a difficulty baseline. Third, we introduce key-alignment: at inference we estimate the stored forward key for the target's known forward fact and inject/rotate the reverse-query representation toward it at the retrieval layer, testing whether reverse recall is restored without weight edits, with false-positive controls on facts the model genuinely does not store. Experiments span Pythia, Qwen2.5, and Llama-3 across scales and synthetic controlled-fact injection, characterizing whether key asymmetry shrinks with scale.
Experiments: 1) DATASETS: (a) Natural relational facts from CounterFact/T-REx with clear inverse relations (parent/child, capital-of/country-of, authored/author-of, located-in/contains), instantiated in matched FORWARD ('A's mother is __' -> B) and REVERSE ('B is the mother of __' -> A) forms with the same underlying edge. (b) A synthetic controlled set: inject ~1k novel fictional (A, r, B) facts via continued fine-tuning on Pythia/Qwen small models, training ONLY the forward direction, giving ground-truth over what was learned. Restrict analysis to facts the model answers correctly in the forward direction (fact demonstrably stored). 2) KEY EXTRACTION & VALIDATION: On forward queries, use activation patching (clean vs corrupted source entity, and separately corrupted target) to localize the layers/positions whose residual carries the fact to the answer; extract a candidate key as the difference-of-means / top principal directions of the source+relation-position residual at the peak retrieval layer. Validate SUFFICIENCY (patching only the key direction transports the correct answer) and TARGET-BLINDNESS (target-position or target-token directions do NOT reconstruct the key; corrupting the target barely changes the key). 3) KEY-DISTANCE PREDICTS REVERSAL: For each fact, compute the key produced by the reverse query and by indirect paraphrases; measure cosine distance to the stored forward key. Test whether key-distance predicts reverse-recall failure (AUROC on held-out relations) and report incremental AUROC over a difficulty-only baseline (entity frequency, forward logit margin, answer token frequency). Predict: successful reverse recall (when it occurs) coincides with small key-distance. 4) CAUSAL LINK TO REVERSAL CURSE: On the synthetic forward-only-trained set (guaranteed reversal curse), verify the reverse query yields a mismatched key and that no forward key is retrievable from the reverse cue; contrast with facts trained bidirectionally. 5) KEY-ALIGNMENT INTERVENTION: At inference on a reverse query, estimate the stored forward key (from the target entity's known forward fact representation) and inject/rotate the reverse-query residual toward it at the retrieval layer (scaled by alpha). Measure REVERSE-RECALL RECOVERY RATE, FALSE-POSITIVE rate on facts the model does not store (must not hallucinate a confident inverse), and SIDE EFFECTS on unrelated correctly-answered forward queries. Baselines: no intervention, random-direction injection, few-shot reverse examples, CoT. 6) SCALING/GENERALIZATION: Repeat across Pythia (410M/1.4B/6.9B), Qwen2.5 (0.5B/7B), Llama-3 (8B); test whether key asymmetry and recovery transfer across relation types and shrink with scale. METRICS: key sufficiency/target-blindness patching effects, key-distance predictive & incremental AUROC, reverse-recall recovery rate, false-positive rate, side-effect accuracy delta, scaling/relation-transfer trends.
Risk Factors and Limitations: 1) The 'key' may not be cleanly low-dimensional or may be polysemantic; we report the dimensionality needed for sufficiency and treat a graded rather than single-direction key as still informative. 2) Linear-probe/patching decodability could be an artifact; sufficiency and target-blindness are causal patching tests, not just decoding claims. 3) Reverse-recall failures may partly reflect genuine absence of the inverse fact rather than a key mismatch; the synthetic forward-only-trained set controls for this by guaranteeing the edge exists. 4) The key-alignment intervention risks inducing confident wrong inverses (e.g., non-injective relations where B has many possible A); we measure false-positive rate and restrict primary evaluation to functional/near-injective relations. 5) Estimating the stored forward key at inference requires knowing the target's forward fact, which is available for evaluation but limits deployment scope; we frame the intervention as a mechanistic probe of reversibility, not a production fix. 6) Effects may be architecture-specific (GQA vs MHA) and scale-dependent; we characterize across families rather than assume universality.
